topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; competency frameworks may require adaptation for Australian healthcare settings and regulatory environments.
takeaways: Identifies core digital competencies needed in public health roles, providing a structured reference point for assessing gaps in your workforce's AI and digital capabilities.

European framework may offer useful benchmarks, but Australian organisations should cross-reference with local health sector standards and regulatory requirements (e.g., AHPRA, state health departments) before implementation.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty development context; applicability to other sectors or non-academic organisations requires clarification of the study's geographic and institutional scope.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption can be reframed as a readiness problem; structured development programs that build confidence and competence may be more effective than top-down mandates.
Targeted professional development for educators is essential before expecting them to teach AI literacy to students — ensure trainers model the behaviours and skills they expect learners to develop.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - journals.sagepub.com
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  journals.sagepub.com
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on Generation Z cohort; geographic scope and educational contexts not specified in snippet. Findings may not generalise to older workers or non-traditional learning environments.
takeaways: Design AI literacy programs specifically for younger workers entering the job market, emphasising practical skills that complement (rather than replace) domain expertise.

Incorporate 'innovative educational strategies' — likely referring to hands-on projects, real-world case studies, or experiential learning — rather than traditional classroom instruction to engage Generation Z learners.
Address the AI skills gap proactively by integrating AI literacy into secondary and tertiary education curricula before workers enter organisations.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG perspective based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect client base which tends toward larger organisations in developed economies.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability-building initiative, not just a technology rollout — this shifts focus from tools to the skills and mindsets employees need to work effectively alongside AI systems.
Assess your current workforce's AI literacy gaps systematically before implementation; tailor upskilling programs to different roles rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

Plan for role transformation and potential workforce restructuring as part of AI strategy — proactive communication about which roles will change, which will be created, and which will be displaced helps reduce anxiety and build buy-in.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development unclear without seeing full methodology and geographic scope.
takeaways: Consider embedding AI competencies within a broader digital literacy framework rather than teaching AI in isolation — this holistic approach may improve knowledge retention and transfer to real-world contexts.

Middle school foundational competencies (e.g. understanding data, algorithmic thinking, bias recognition) can serve as a baseline model for designing AI literacy programs for adult employees with varying technical backgrounds.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on higher education sector; generalisability to workplace AI literacy development in organisational settings unclear without access to full article.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your employee roles (technical, domain-specific, or general literacy) before designing training, rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach.

Consider whether higher education pedagogical strategies (project-based learning, interdisciplinary approaches) can be adapted to your organisational context to improve employee AI capability development.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability is limited without access to full methodology — sample size, geographic location, sector, and study design are unclear from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key mechanism through which employees translate AI tools into innovation — consider assessing and developing these capacities in teams adopting AI.

Framing AI as a 'job resource' rather than a threat may unlock greater creative problem-solving and willingness to experiment with new technologies, suggesting messaging and change management approaches matter significantly.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professional groups. Geographic scope not evident from title/snippet; sample size and country of origin unclear without full article access.
takeaways: Organisations introducing AI in healthcare should actively protect and expand nurse autonomy in decision-making — the data suggest autonomy is a critical buffer between AI implementation and employee wellbeing outcomes.

Assess AI readiness not just in terms of technical skills, but also measure and address staff concerns about loss of control; wellbeing impacts depend on how much autonomy workers retain alongside new AI tools.

When rolling out medical AI, monitor wellbeing longitudinally rather than at a single time point — the three-wave design suggests effects may unfold over time, requiring sustained attention to autonomy and psychological safety.

articles.title: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on HBR analysis and likely case examples, but specific sample characteristics, size, and geographic scope are not stated in the snippet. Findings may reflect primarily US/Western organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify employee traits or prior experiences that predict who will benefit most from AI tools for creative work, then target upskilling and implementation strategies accordingly rather than assuming uniform adoption outcomes.

Examine whether employees view AI as a collaborative partner versus a threat; those with psychological safety to experiment and reframe AI as augmenting (not replacing) their ideas are more likely to unlock creative gains.

Assess and address potential barriers to creative AI use — such as lack of prompt-writing skills, discomfort with ambiguity, or fear of job displacement — through targeted coaching and clear messaging about creative roles AI cannot fill.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full methodology, cannot assess sample size, sector coverage, or geographic scope. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) may apply broadly, but specific findings' applicability depends on study design details.
takeaways: Generative AI can either reduce employee knowledge-building (automation effect) or enhance it (augmentation effect) depending on how it's deployed — consider whether your AI tools are designed to replace thinking or to extend capability.

Understanding the paradox helps explain why some teams struggle with knowledge retention after adopting AI, while others see improved learning — audit current AI usage to identify which effect is dominating in your organisation.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geography, and sector not specified. Findings on paternalistic leadership may have limited applicability in Western organisations with flatter hierarchies; more common in East Asian contexts.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — those who feel genuine ownership of AI systems are more likely to actively collaborate with and adapt them to their work (AI crafting), rather than resisting or underutilising them.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, emphasise the leader's role as a supportive mentor who guides employees through AI adoption; this creates the relational foundation needed for employees to develop ownership and engagement with AI.

Create space for 'AI crafting' — allowing employees to customise, configure, or shape how AI tools fit their specific workflows — as a mechanism to translate psychological ownership into active, productive collaboration.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone, but likely limited to the specific organisational sample studied. Generalisability depends on sample size, sector diversity, and geographic scope — not evident from title/snippet. Findings may not transfer across different cultural contexts or industries with varying AI adoption rates.
takeaways: Develop self-efficacy in AI tools among employees through targeted training and hands-on practice — this protective factor can reduce job insecurity when AI is introduced.

Leaders should adopt transformational leadership behaviours (inspiring vision, individualised support, intellectual stimulation) when deploying AI, as this leadership style moderates the negative effect of AI on job security perceptions.
Job insecurity from AI is not inevitable — organisational interventions targeting both individual capability (self-efficacy) and leadership approach can significantly buffer employee anxiety.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework is based on consulting experience with large organisations, likely skewed toward multinational enterprises and developed economies, but specific case studies or validation data are not evident from the snippet.
takeaways: Shift mindset from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (behavioural and cultural change) to increase likelihood of sustainable employee engagement with AI tools.
Design change interventions that explicitly target human behaviours and mindsets alongside technical rollout, rather than treating them as separate workstreams.

Use Deloitte's change approach as a structured template to identify which employee behaviours need to shift for your organisation's specific AI use case, then build targeted support around those behaviours.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical sample or geographic scope. Insights may reflect Silicon Valley bias and may not generalise across all sectors or geographic regions.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are likely to be augmented vs. displaced by AI, and use this to plan targeted upskilling interventions before disruption occurs.

Frame AI adoption as a behaviour change challenge requiring clear communication about how roles will evolve, not disappear — resistance often stems from uncertainty about job security rather than technical barriers.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Further examination of the methodology section would be needed to assess geographic scope, sector coverage, and sample representativeness.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger either approach (seeking new opportunities) or avoidance (withdrawing from tasks) responses in employees — understanding which response your team exhibits helps you design targeted interventions to encourage adaptive job crafting.

When introducing AI, explicitly communicate how roles will evolve and create opportunities for employees to shape their work around new technologies, rather than passively accepting changes, to shift behaviour from avoidance toward approach.

Monitor psychological safety and clarity during AI rollout; employees who feel threatened or uncertain are more likely to avoid engaging with AI tools, while those who see upskilling pathways are more likely to actively craft their roles around new capabilities.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on client work across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption initiatives as workforce transformation programs, not just technology implementations, to secure buy-in from employees and managers who may otherwise perceive AI as a threat to their roles.

Design change management strategies that address skill gaps and role redefinition in parallel with AI tool deployment, rather than treating workforce adaptation as an afterthought to technical rollout.

Build capability-building and role clarity into the change process from the outset — employees are more likely to embrace AI when they understand how their work will evolve and have pathways to develop relevant skills.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese primary and secondary school context. Findings may not generalise to other educational systems with different institutional structures, teacher training approaches, or cultural attitudes toward technology adoption.
takeaways: AI tools can paradoxically increase teaching innovation when framed as challenging opportunities, but decrease it when perceived as threatening—frame AI adoption messaging around capability-building rather than job displacement or competency concerns.

Teacher psychological safety and perception of autonomy are critical: identify and address underlying anxieties about AI before implementation, as threat perception may trigger defensive responses that inhibit experimentation with new teaching methods.

Context matters significantly—sector, school resources, and institutional support for experimentation will influence whether teachers view AI as a lever for innovation or a constraint, so tailor change management to local school conditions rather than one-size-fits-all rollout.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey insights draw on global client work but are not based on peer-reviewed research or controlled studies. Findings reflect consulting practice rather than empirical validation, though frameworks may apply broadly across sectors.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as organizational change management rather than isolated training delivery—this shifts focus from individual capability gaps to systemic barriers, change resistance, and leadership alignment that drive adoption.

Identify and address the psychological and structural factors preventing skill adoption (e.g., fear of displacement, unclear relevance to role) rather than assuming training completion alone drives behaviour change.

Design upskilling interventions with clear, role-specific application pathways and early wins to build momentum and credibility—abstract or deferred value propositions reduce engagement and persistence.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — appears to report on recent psychology research but geographic scope and sample details are not provided in the available text.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissists may have an unexpected edge in early romantic attraction, challenging the assumption that narcissistic traits universally repel potential partners.

The finding is counterintuitive: traits typically associated with arrogance and lack of empathy apparently work in some contexts, raising questions about what initially draws people to narcissistic personalities.
This highlights the gap between short-term mating appeal and long-term relationship quality — initial romantic 'success' doesn't necessarily predict relationship health or stability.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from title and snippet alone; likely limited to laboratory conditions with controlled surprise stimuli, which may not reflect real-world unexpected events.
takeaways: People don't all remember surprising moments the same way — your personality shapes which unexpected events stick with you and which you forget, revealing why eyewitness accounts vary so much.
Introverts and extroverts may encode surprise differently in memory, suggesting our natural temperament acts like a filter that determines what our brain deems worth remembering.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven summary without access to underlying research methodology, sample size, or geographic scope. Original study details are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies continue to find structural and functional differences in individuals with psychopathic traits, challenging the idea that personality differences are purely behavioural.
The 'shocking difference' framing highlights how neuroscience discoveries about atypical brains capture public imagination, even when the practical implications remain unclear.
These kinds of findings raise interesting questions about biological determinism — do brain differences explain behaviour, or do they just correlate with it?

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope, sample size, and methodology details not provided.
takeaways: Wine review language contains hidden personality signals that AI can detect — suggesting our everyday writing style reveals more about who we are than we realize.

The finding is surprisingly fun because it shows machines can spot personality patterns in something as seemingly trivial as how we describe taste, hinting that personality is woven into everything we write.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - cam.ac.uk
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  cam.ac.uk
articles.generalisability: Likely high — appears to be a cross-cultural analysis, though specific sample details are unclear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: Your music taste may be a surprisingly universal personality marker — people with similar traits gravitate toward similar genres regardless of where they're from.
This suggests personality and music preference are linked at a fundamental level, not just shaped by local culture or upbringing.
A fun conversation starter: your Spotify playlist might reveal more about your personality to a stranger from another country than you'd expect.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Twin studies typically reveal heritability patterns within specific populations but findings may not generalise across different cultural, political, or socioeconomic contexts where authoritarianism is expressed differently.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs have a significant genetic component — meaning your genes influence your tendency toward authoritarianism roughly as much as your upbringing does, which surprises many people who assume it's purely learned.

This doesn't mean authoritarianism is 'hardwired' — genetics loads the gun but environment pulls the trigger, so the same genetic predisposition can lead to wildly different outcomes depending on what political and social messaging someone is exposed to.

The finding challenges the intuition that political beliefs are simply chosen or taught, suggesting instead that personality traits linked to genes (like preference for order, distrust of outsiders, or need for security) naturally gravitate toward authoritarian ideologies.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on academic teams in multicultural settings; findings may not generalise to corporate or other organisational contexts, and the specific role of AI in inclusive leadership requires further research across diverse sectors.
takeaways: AI tools can potentially support inclusive leadership practices by identifying and mitigating gender bias in team dynamics, but success depends on how leaders interpret and act on algorithmic recommendations rather than blindly following them.

In multicultural academic teams, algorithmic support for inclusion must account for intersecting identities (gender, cultural background) to avoid reinforcing existing hierarchies or creating new algorithmic biases.

Leaders should treat AI-assisted inclusion as a complement to, not replacement for, developing their own inclusive leadership capabilities and fostering psychological safety through genuine dialogue and accountability.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate — PwC's global survey reaches a broad geographic scope, but sample composition, weighting methodology, and specific sector representation are not detailed in the snippet. Results may reflect perspectives of workers in PwC's client base and English-speaking regions more heavily.
takeaways: Use workforce sentiment data to benchmark psychological safety concerns in your organisation against global trends; identify whether fears around AI, job security, or workplace culture align with broader patterns that might require proactive communication.
Psychological safety depends partly on transparency about organisational change — ensure leaders communicate honestly about AI adoption and workforce changes to reduce anxiety-driven disengagement.
Track shifts in employee 'hopes and fears' over time within your own organisation to detect emerging psychological safety risks before they escalate into turnover or reduced engagement.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The mechanisms identified (psychological safety and ethical leadership as mediators between AI adoption and depression) may vary significantly across different organisational contexts, industries, and geographies. Findings may be particularly relevant to high-tech or rapidly digitising sectors.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent attention to psychological safety can increase employee depression risk — leaders implementing AI should proactively establish safe environments where employees can voice concerns, ask questions, and admit skill gaps without fear of negative consequences.

Ethical leadership practices during AI rollout are critical protective factors — organisations should ensure leaders model transparent decision-making about AI use, acknowledge both benefits and risks, and prioritise employee wellbeing alongside efficiency gains.

Monitor psychological safety metrics during AI transitions as an early warning signal for employee mental health impacts, particularly among staff experiencing skill obsolescence fears or role uncertainty.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, methodology, and Australian applicability are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite diverse perspectives and normalise dissent; leaders should model vulnerability and visibly act on employee input to signal that speaking up is safe and valued.
Use psychological safety as an equity lever: employees from underrepresented groups often self-censor more; deliberate safety practices can reduce this gap and improve inclusion outcomes.
Measure psychological safety regularly (through surveys or focus groups) and track it alongside performance metrics to demonstrate its link to business outcomes and justify continued investment.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — advice is generic and applicable across most organisational contexts, though SHRM's US focus means examples and regulatory references may not directly translate to Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Identify and apply the specific leader behaviours the article recommends (e.g., inviting input, acknowledging mistakes, responding non-defensively) to model psychological safety in your team interactions.

Use the four recommended approaches as a diagnostic framework to audit gaps in your current team's psychological safety, then prioritise which lever to pull first based on your team's specific pain points.

Recognise that psychological safety is built through repeated, consistent leader actions—not one-off communications—so establish regular practices (e.g., blameless retrospectives, explicitly inviting dissenting views) to reinforce it over time.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — article title and snippet alone do not provide sufficient methodological detail to assess sample size, geographic scope, or sector specificity. Full text review needed to determine generalisability.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) as a foundation for employees to view AI tools as enablers rather than threats, which can unlock innovation potential in algorithm-driven roles.

Design AI integration programmes that explicitly support employee confidence and problem-solving capacity, as psychological readiness appears to mediate the relationship between AI availability and innovative outcomes.
Assess and strengthen staff resilience and optimism before or during AI adoption, since these psychological resources may be key to helping workers adapt productively to algorithmic workflows.
